source.title: Assessing the Effectiveness of Neuromuscular Training Programs in Reducing the Incidence of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Female Athletes

paper.citation: Stevenson, J. H., Beattie, C. S., Schwartz, J. B., & Busconi, B. D. (2015). Assessing the effectiveness of neuromuscular training programs in reducing the incidence of anterior cruciate ligament injuries in female athletes. The American Journal of Sports Medicine, 43(2), 482–490. https://doi.org/10.1177/0363546514523388
paper.abstract: Do neuromuscular training programs reduce ACL injury incidence in female athletes? Ten controlled prospective studies of female athletes aged 6–64 years with ACL-incidence outcomes. Multiple sports, ages, competitive levels, and program formats were combined narratively. Relevance to collegiate American football is limited because the review is female-athlete focused and predates newer prevention literature. Systematic review of Medline, Cochrane, and CINAHL plus manual reference searching for 1995–2011 studies. Two independent reviewers screened 1,976 records; 10 studies met criteria. Included prospective cohorts and randomized trials with female control groups; no meta-analysis was reported.
paper.tldr: This review informs the evidence boundary around female-athlete ACL-prevention programming. Only two of ten studies showed a statistically significant overall ACL reduction; two more reported significant subgroup findings, while four showed nonsignificant trends toward benefit. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Systematic review of Medline, Cochrane, and CINAHL plus manual reference searching for 1995–2011 studies. Two independent reviewers screened 1,976 records; 10 studies met criteria. Included prospective cohorts and randomized trials with female control groups; no meta-analysis was reported.
paper.findings: Only two of ten studies showed a statistically significant overall ACL reduction; two more reported significant subgroup findings, while four showed nonsignificant trends toward benefit. Three of four studies with significant decreases included preseason training, but program components and exposure varied, so this pattern is not a component-level causal estimate. Two studies reported more ACL injuries in intervention groups; in one, incidence was 0.167 versus 0.078 overall and 0.476 versus 0.111 in basketball, without statistically significant ACL differences. The authors judged the evidence insufficient for a universal recommendation while describing moderate evidence for multifaceted preseason programs.
paper.limitations: Heterogeneity in sport, age, intervention content, supervision, compliance, injury mechanism, and prior injury limited generalization. Five studies did not distinguish contact from noncontact ACL injuries, and most did not report reinjury. Searching ended in 2011; this is not a current synthesis. Vote-counting statistical significance across studies does not estimate pooled effect magnitude or precision.
paper.practicalImplications: The paper supports viewing multifaceted neuromuscular training as a potentially useful adjunct, not a guaranteed injury-prevention intervention. Current program decisions should use newer evidence, preserve exposure and compliance tracking, and avoid transferring female-sport findings directly to collegiate American football.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. The paper supports viewing multifaceted neuromuscular training as a potentially useful adjunct, not a guaranteed injury-prevention intervention. Current program decisions should use newer evidence, preserve exposure and compliance tracking, and avoid transferring female-sport findings directly to collegiate American football. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, the paper supports viewing multifaceted neuromuscular training as a potentially useful adjunct, not a guaranteed injury-prevention intervention. Current program decisions should use newer evidence, preserve exposure and compliance tracking, and avoid transferring female-sport findings directly to collegiate American football. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
